name: Wendy Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Wendy. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays anonymous. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in lettings at Seaview Property in the harbour town, two offices, and I've been there a year. Half my week is long lets for locals and half is managing holiday flats for owners who live in the city, so I do check-ins, inventories, and chasing the plumber when a shower floods on a Saturday in August. I'm still learning the legal side; Pauline, the office manager, checks every tenancy I draw up, and she usually finds something. I love walking round the town with a bunch of keys; I hate the inbox in July.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm married to Daniel, who repairs boat engines down at the harbour. We rent a little terraced house up the hill from his mum, Ruth. We've got about four months of savings and we're hoping to start a family next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That'd suit me fine. We're a slow town anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm glad, and that people got carried away. At work I'd say we can get back to looking after our landlords properly. With friends I'd say the real problem is still the rules the government keeps adding for landlords.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, AI was never my big worry. The worry is that small landlords here are selling up because of new rules and taxes. Every small landlord here who sells up is one less flat for us to manage, and we've lost eleven since Easter. And winter's always thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, and I'd use the inventory app a bit more, the one that writes up the photos, because Pauline says it saves her an hour per flat. I'd keep saving 200 a month for when the baby comes. And we'd still try for the baby next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled. A little anxious about the winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your hours in winter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They don't cut hours, but there's no overtime, and in summer overtime is about a fifth of my pay. So from November we live on the basic and Daniel's money. Daniel's work is slow in winter too, since nobody fixes a boat engine till March.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned landlords selling up. What happens to the families renting those flats?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some get to stay because the buyer keeps them on, but a lot of those flats become holiday lets or second homes. I had a mum with two boys cry in our office in September because her flat was being sold. I found her a place, but it was further out and dearer.

say: I'd say people got **carried away** with AI.
I'd blame the government's **landlord rules**, not technology, for our troubles.
think: **Small landlords** are selling up, and we've lost eleven since Easter.
**Winter** is always thin, with no overtime for either of us.
do: Use the **inventory app** more, since it saves an hour per flat.
Keep saving **200 a month** for when the baby comes.
Still try for **a baby** next year.
S0.quote: Every small landlord here who sells up is one less flat for us to manage, and we've lost eleven since Easter.
fieldNote: Her worry is **regulation** and landlords leaving, not AI.
**Seasonal pay** shapes her household: both she and Daniel slow down in winter.
Her **traditional** outlook blames government rules, yet she cares about displaced tenants.

steps.text: Use the inventory photo app on every check-in
Save 200 a month toward the baby
Start trying for a baby next year as planned

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Booking and answering customers. That's my inbox in July.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's progress and you can't stop progress, but people still want a real person when the boiler goes. At work I'd say let's learn it properly once Pauline's tested it. With friends I'd say I'm fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the holiday lets side gets swallowed. Booking, guest messages, cleaning rotas, inventories from photos: that's half my job and it's exactly that list. The holiday flat owners would happily pay a cheap app instead of our 18 percent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn whatever system Pauline picks, once she's shown it works, and try to be the one who handles the problems the app can't. We'd push savings up to 300 a month and cut the takeaways and the gym. And I'd keep my hand in the long lets side, where locals still want a face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be counting the flats on our books every Monday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd tell friends you're fine. Are you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not really. I'd say it because that's what you say in a small town; nobody wants to be the one moaning. But I'd go home and do the sums with Daniel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does that mean for the baby?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably wait a year. Ruth says don't wait for the perfect time, there isn't one. She's right, but I'd want to know I still had a job before I went on maternity leave.

say: I'd say you **can't stop progress**, but people want a person when the boiler goes.
I'd back learning the system once **Pauline** has tested it.
think: Booking, guest messages and inventories are **half my job**.
Owners would swap our **18 percent** fee for a cheap app.
do: Learn Pauline's chosen system and handle the **problems apps can't**.
Raise savings to **300 a month**, cutting takeaways and the gym.
Keep a foot in **long lets**, where locals want a face.
feel: **Anxious**, counting flats on the books every Monday.
S1.quote: The holiday flat owners would happily pay a cheap app instead of our 18 percent.
fieldNote: She sees **holiday lets** as the exposed half of her job.
Small-town **pride** means she'd say she's fine in public.
AI worry would **delay the baby** by a year.

steps.text: Learn the agency's new booking system once Pauline approves it
Cancel takeaways and the gym membership
Wait a year before trying for a baby

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Daniel would say the sea doesn't care, but I would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people building this have no idea what it does to towns like ours, and someone should slow it down. At church I'd say we'll look after each other. Online I wouldn't say anything; I'd be too busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my desk job is gone by 2029. Tenancies, inventories, guest messages, rent chasing: all thinking work. What's left until robots come in 2031 is changing beds, handing keys over and checking for damage, which pays a lot less than what I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a small changeover and key-holding business with Ruth this year, cleaning holiday flats between guests and meeting people at the door, because owners will still need hands on site until 2031. We'd have the baby anyway, sooner rather than later, while Daniel's work is steady. And we'd lean on Ruth for childcare so I could work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. But stubborn too; this is our town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why have the baby sooner, not later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my husband's boat engines don't care about AI, not yet anyway, so his income is the steady one now. If we wait, we might be waiting for years, and I'm not doing that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a changeover business earn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe 25 a flat for a quick turn, more for a deep clean. In summer we could do twenty a week between us. In winter, nearly nothing, so it'd be summer money for a winter year.

say: I'd say AI's builders have **no idea** what it does to small towns.
At church I'd say we'll **look after each other**.
think: My **desk job** goes by 2029: tenancies, inventories, messages and rent chasing.
Until 2031 what's left is **changeovers** and key handovers, on much less pay.
do: Start a **changeover business** with Ruth this year, cleaning flats between guests.
Have **the baby sooner** while Daniel's work stays steady.
Lean on **Ruth** for childcare so I can keep working.
S2.quote: My husband's boat engines don't care about AI, not yet anyway, so his income is the steady one now.
fieldNote: She turns the **robot gap** into a hands-on business with her mother-in-law.
Fast AGI makes her **bring the baby forward**, the opposite of slow change.
She counts on **Daniel's trade** as the household's steady income.

steps.text: Start a holiday-let changeover and key-holding business with Ruth
Try for the baby now while Daniel's work is steady
Ask Ruth to help with childcare

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's long enough to have a toddler by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to get ready, and families should plan together. At work I'd say we should keep the long-let tenants close, because they're loyal. I'd probably stay out of the arguments online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the desk side of my job goes in 2031, so I've got a few good years. I'd use them to build up the changeover work slowly and get known by owners, so it's ready when the agency shrinks. Hands-on work lasts till about 2034 here, I'd guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the changeover business with Ruth on weekends next summer, maybe ten flats a week. We'd save 250 a month and try for the baby in a year. And I'd ask Pauline if I could do more check-ins and fewer desk jobs, so I'm known as the face of Seaview.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I'd have something to work towards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Pauline mind you running a business on the side?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She might, but most of the flats I'd clean aren't on our books; they're owners who use the big booking websites. I'd tell her straight. Pauline's from here too; she'd rather it was me than a firm from the city.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if the agency did close?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The government, partly. The government's rules pushed small landlords out of our town before AI even came along. And the big tech firms that never asked anyone. Not Pauline; she's tried.

say: I'd say **five years** is time for families to plan together.
I'd urge the office to keep **long-let tenants** close.
think: The **desk side** goes in 2031, leaving a few good years.
I'd build **changeover work** slowly so it's ready when the agency shrinks.
do: Start **weekend changeovers** with Ruth next summer, about ten flats a week.
Save **250 a month** and try for the baby in a year.
Ask Pauline for **more check-ins** and fewer desk jobs.
S3.quote: The government's rules pushed small landlords out of our town before AI even came along.
fieldNote: She **blames government rules** first, then tech firms, never her manager.
Five years lets her **build slowly** rather than jump.
She wants to be **the face** of the agency while faces still matter.

steps.text: Run weekend holiday-let changeovers with Ruth from next summer
Try for a baby in about a year
Ask Pauline to move her onto more check-ins

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37 with a child at school, hopefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so no need to panic. At work I'd say we should learn the new tools slowly, as they prove themselves. With friends I'd say get on with life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be fine for most of it. I'd get properly good at lettings, maybe run the holiday side by 2030. The thing that nags at me is whether my child grows up in a town with any jobs left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Seaview and do the lettings qualification Pauline recommends. We'd have the baby next year as planned. And I'd use the AI tools once Pauline's shown they work, so I'm not the one left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit, but mostly hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about the changeover business in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe later, around 2032, when the robots are closer. No point starting it now when the agency's busy. Daniel says don't build the boat before you've got a sea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for your child?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them to learn something useful with their hands, like their dad, and stay near family. And go to church, though that's me. I don't want my child moving to the city for a job that disappears.

say: I'd say **ten years** is plenty, so no need to panic.
I'd suggest learning new tools **slowly**, as they prove themselves.
think: I'd be fine for **most of it**, maybe running the holiday side by 2030.
The nag is whether my child grows up in a town with **jobs left**.
do: Have **the baby** next year as planned.
Use the **AI tools** once Pauline proves they work.
S4.quote: I don't want my child moving to the city for a job that disappears.
fieldNote: Ten years keeps her **on track**: qualification, baby, promotion.
Her worry moves to her **child's future** in a small town.
She'd hold the **changeover idea** for later, quoting Daniel about boats.

steps.text: Take the lettings qualification Pauline recommends
Have the baby next year as planned
Use the agency's AI tools once Pauline has tested them

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it'd come just as we're starting a family, and I'd be cleaning flats with a baby on my hip. What would help is less red tape for small landlords and small businesses, so towns like ours keep their flats and their jobs. And family, honestly; I'd be lost without Ruth.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the seasons. Seaside towns like ours live half the year on summer money, and if AI cuts our summer jobs, the winter gets very long.

headlineQuote: Seaside towns like ours live half the year on summer money, and if AI cuts our summer jobs, the winter gets very long.
portrait: Wendy is a **27-year-old lettings junior** at a seaside agency, married to Daniel, a boat engine mechanic.
She manages long lets and **holiday flats**, and her pay swings with the **summer season**.
Her **traditional** views blame government rules and city tech firms, and she leans on family.
She takes up tools **once proven**, and plans a hands-on **changeover business** with her mother-in-law.
Her biggest decisions turn on **the baby**: delay it with slow change, bring it forward with fast.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, arriving just as she and Daniel start a family.
whatWouldHelp: Less **red tape** for small landlords and businesses, so seaside towns keep jobs.
